title: Which Door Am I At: A Belief Over Places, and Why It Must Never Say Never

questions.question: A robot wakes up in a corridor of identical doors. Why can one number and a spread not describe where it is?
options: It might be at several separate places, and one number and a spread describe one lump: after one reading of a door the belief had 9 places near the top
questions.explanation: A belief over places can be at several at once.

questions.question: What does moving do to a belief?
options: Spreads it out by the slip: all of it at place 5, moved one place with 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1, gave 0.10, 0.80 and 0.10

questions.question: What does sensing do?
options: Multiplies each place by how believable the reading makes it and normalises: after one door reading each door was 0.0938 and each wall 0.0104
questions.explanation: The prediction was worked out by hand.

questions.question: What happens to a belief whose places have all been ruled out?
options: It goes back to knowing nothing, 1/24 each, rather than dividing by a sum of zero
questions.explanation: Normalise guards against a sum that is zero or not a number.

questions.question: A belief is told the sensor never errs and then gets one wrong reading. What happens?
options: The true place is multiplied by zero, the belief is wiped out and resets: 0.042 of the true place and 5 steps to recover, against 1.000 and 1 step for a belief that allowed a 1 percent error
questions.explanation: A probability of zero says something is impossible.

questions.question: In 200 trips with a sensor wrong 1 time in 20, which description of the sensor did best?
options: About right, 0.05 to 0.10 for a wrong reading: 0.710 and 0.715 found the place, against 0.625 for never wrong and 0.050 for a sensor that says nothing
questions.explanation: Too confident and too sceptical are both worse.
